subject: biology
title: Classification of living organisms
key_idea: Living things are sorted into groups. Linnaeus used seven groups from kingdom to species, and gave each organism a two-part name. New evidence from microscopes, biochemistry and DNA led to the three-domain system. Evolutionary trees show how organisms are related.

blocks.text: Carl Linnaeus classified living things in the 1700s, by their appearance. This section covers his groups and how organisms are named.

items.meaning: Sorting living things into groups, depending on their structure and characteristics.
A two-part name made of the genus and the species, for example Musca domestica (the house fly).

blocks.text: There are seven groups, from largest to smallest. Tap each group, using the house fly as the example.

diagram.alt: Tap each Linnaean group to see where it comes in the order and the house fly's group.

parts.name: Kingdom
parts.detail: The largest of the seven groups. The house fly is in the kingdom Animalia.

parts.name: Phylum
parts.detail: The group after kingdom. The house fly is in the phylum Arthropoda.

parts.name: Class
parts.detail: The group after phylum. The house fly is in the class Insecta.

parts.name: Order
parts.detail: The group after class. The house fly is in the order Diptera.

parts.name: Family
parts.detail: The group after order. The house fly is in the family Muscidae.

parts.name: Genus
parts.detail: The group after family. It is the first part of the binomial name: Musca.

parts.name: Species
parts.detail: The smallest group. It is the second part of the binomial name: domestica.

diagram.prompt: The seven groups, largest to smallest

items: The order is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
The binomial name is the genus and the species.

sections.heading: New evidence and the three-domain system

blocks.text: Linnaeus used appearance. Better evidence has since changed how we classify. This section covers the new evidence and the new system.

items: Internal and cell structures, seen with **light and electron microscopes**.
Chemical analysis and comparison of **biochemical processes**.
**DNA and genetic analysis**.
Studies of evolutionary relationships.

blocks.text: Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system, based on DNA and chemical evidence. A domain is a larger group than a kingdom.

rows: Primitive bacteria. They can survive in extreme environments.
Organisms whose cells have a nucleus: protists, fungi, plants and animals.

blocks.text: Before this, living things were often sorted into five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes. Genetic analysis led to the three domains. For example, Archaea DNA is more like that of eukaryotes.

items: New evidence, especially DNA, changed classification.
The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota.
Plants, animals, fungi and protists are all in the domain Eukaryota.

blocks.text: Evolutionary trees show how organisms are related. This section covers how genes are compared.

items: An **evolutionary tree** shows how scientists believe organisms are related.
It uses current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
Species whose branches split from a common ancestor more recently are more closely related.
Scientists compare the **sequence of genes** from different organisms.
Closely related organisms have more similar sequences. Organisms with similar gene sequences share a recent common ancestor.
Differences in sequence can show how far back two species split.
The same idea works for the amino acid sequence of a protein. The species with the fewest differences from an ancestor is the most closely related.
In **molecular phylogenetics**, DNA sequencing is used to work out evolutionary relationships.
A **natural** classification groups organisms by their evolutionary relationships.
An **artificial** classification groups them using chosen features, whether or not they are closely related.
More similar gene sequences mean a closer relationship.
Molecular phylogenetics uses DNA sequences to classify organisms.

checks.q: What are the two parts of a binomial name?
Give three types of evidence now used to classify living things, other than appearance.
checks.a: Any three from: internal or cell structures with light or electron microscopes, chemical analysis, comparison of biochemical processes, DNA or genetic analysis, studies of evolutionary relationships.

checks.q: Two species have gene sequences that are very similar. What does this suggest?
checks.a: They are closely related and share a recent common ancestor.

worked_example.question:
Carl Woese developed the three-domain system of classification.

Describe the three-domain system of classification.
answer_points: It is based on DNA or chemical evidence.
Archaea are primitive or simple bacteria.
Prokaryota (Bacteria) are true or modern bacteria.
Eukaryota includes plants and animals (organisms whose cells have a nucleus).
worked_example.tip: Any three of the four points score one mark each.

worked_example.question:
Genetic analysis provides evidence for evolution.
Scientists can sequence genes from different organisms.

Describe how this type of genetic analysis provides evidence for evolution.
answer_points: Compare the genes, or the sequence of genes, from different organisms.
Closely related organisms have more similar or identical sequences, and differences in sequence can show evolution.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the comparison, one for what it shows.

worked_example.question: Describe what is meant by the term species.
answer_points: A group of organisms that can reproduce.

items.meaning: A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
